content.title: About
content.content: Candied apple is a whole apple coated with a thin layer of sweet caramel. Apples are usually selected from firm varieties so they keep their shape during processing. The caramel gives the fruit a bright golden color, a sweet aroma and a crunchy shell, while the inside remains juicy and slightly tart.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Candied apples are a classic fall street snack in the United States and Canada.
Traditionally the apples are dipped in a caramel made from sugar, butter and cream, often flavored with vanilla or cinnamon.
In Japan a similar treat exists, where the coating is flavored with soy sauce and ginger.
Candied apples are a staple at fairs, parks and festivals, where they are eaten straight without removing the caramel shell.
There is also a chocolate‑coated version, where caramel is replaced by melted chocolate.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Apples provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, which supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Fresh apple flesh supplies vitamin C, an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Apple skin is rich in polyphenols that may reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: The sugar in the caramel raises blood glucose rapidly, making it a handy snack for physical activity.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Sweet flavors can stimulate serotonin production, enhancing mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The caramel makes the product very calorie‑dense and raises its glycemic index, which may be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Caramel coating can be extremely hot right after preparation; allow it to cool before handling.

items.title: Apple allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to apples or to caramel ingredients such as milk or butter.

items.title: Dental concerns
items.content: Hard caramel can contribute to plaque buildup and cavities with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candied apples are conveniently eaten by hand as a quick snack. They can be sliced for salads, ice cream toppings, or used as decorative elements in desserts. For a softer texture, the apple can be blanched before coating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store finished candied apples in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them: spread on a tray, freeze solid, then transfer to a zip‑lock bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Congee is a traditional Asian rice porridge made by simmering rice in water, broth, or milk until it reaches a smooth, creamy consistency. Its mild flavor makes it a versatile base for both sweet and savory preparations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Congee is considered a comfort food across China, Japan, and Korea, often served to the sick or during recovery.
While short‑grain rice is typical, other grains such as barley, quinoa, or oats can be used.
Japanese versions may include mochi and sweet red bean paste (azuki).
Chinese congee is frequently flavored with pickled vegetables, ginger, and soy sauce.
It can be served sweet (with sugar, fruit, honey) or savory (with meat, seafood, soy sauce).

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture and simple preparation make congee gentle on the digestive system.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides quick‑acting energy, useful for recovery after illness or intense exercise.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Traditional congee is prepared without added fats, fitting low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high liquid content helps maintain proper hydration.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White‑rice congee can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin or gastrointestinal reactions.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: Rice alone does not provide enough protein; adding meat, beans, or eggs is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve congee hot, seasoned with salt, soy sauce, green onions, cooked vegetables, meat, fish, or seafood. For sweet versions, stir in sugar, honey, fresh or dried fruit, or coconut milk. Adjust consistency with additional broth or milk when reheating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked congee to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat on the stove or in a microwave, adding a splash of water or broth to restore the desired texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Dip NFS is a ready‑to‑serve creamy dip made from cream cheese, sour cream and aromatic herbs, designed for quick preparation of snacks and dishes. It has a smooth, slightly tangy flavor with a fresh herb aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Dip NFS was launched in 2015 as part of the “New Flavor Series” line.
The formula contains only natural ingredients and no artificial colors or preservatives.
The cream cheese base is made from whole milk rather than powdered cheese.
The recipe is inspired by Mediterranean dips that often combine yogurt and herbs.
The packaging is made from recyclable plastic, reducing its environmental footprint.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cream cheese is a good source of calcium, which supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: The sour cream component provides live cultures that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The product contains virtually no added sugar, making it suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cream cheese supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: A modest amount of monounsaturated fats in the cheese supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The dip contains dairy, so people with lactose intolerance should consume it cautiously.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey proteins may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The dip has a moderate amount of salt; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the dip refrigerated and use within 5‑7 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dip NFS works well as a sauce for vegetable sticks, chips, crackers, and as a spread for sandwiches, wraps and casseroles. It can be stirred into salads for a creamy texture or used as a base for more complex sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Dip NFS in the refrigerator at 2‑6 °C in its original container. After opening, seal tightly. Do not freeze, as this may alter the texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken enchilada is a classic Mexican dish consisting of corn tortillas filled with cooked chicken, smothered in chili sauce and baked with cheese. It offers a rich, slightly spicy flavor and the aroma of traditional spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “enchilada” comes from the Spanish “enchilar,” meaning “to coat with chili sauce.”
Originally only corn tortillas were used, but today wheat tortillas are also common.
Mexico boasts several regional sauces: red (tomato‑based), green (tomatillo), and black (chipotle).
The dish is traditionally served with rice, beans, and guacamole.
Enchiladas are a staple for celebrations and family gatherings.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin, B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, chicken adds less saturated fat, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Antioxidants in the sauce
items.content: Tomatoes and chili peppers supply lycopene and vitamin C, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Fiber from corn tortillas
items.content: Corn tortillas contribute dietary fiber that aids regular digestion.

items.title: Allergy to corn or dairy
items.content: Tortillas and cheese can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and seasonings are often high in salt; people with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Spiciness of chili
items.content: Hot peppers may irritate the stomach or esophagus in those with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Baking with cheese adds calories; moderation is key for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve enchiladas hot, typically topped with a dollop of sour cream, guacamole, fresh cilantro and a squeeze of lime. They pair well with rice, black beans or a fresh vegetable salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked enchiladas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a sealed bag for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Red cooked peppers are ripe fruits of sweet bell peppers that have been briefly boiled. The cooking process retains most vitamins while giving the flesh a soft, mildly sweet flavor with a hint of smokiness. Cooked peppers are common in salads, soups, stews, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Red peppers contain two to three times more vitamin C than green peppers.
Heat treatment increases the bioavailability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
In many cuisines cooked peppers are served with olive oil and garlic as a simple appetizer.
Cooked peppers retain more moisture and a tender texture compared with dried or roasted varieties.
A pinch of salt can enhance the natural aroma of cooked red peppers.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene protects cells from oxidative stress and may lower the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps you feel full without adding many calories.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6 and folate are involved in protein metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal blood pressure.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to capsaicin or other pepper compounds.

items.title: Excess sodium
items.content: Cooked peppers are often seasoned with salt; over‑consumption can contribute to hypertension.

items.title: Vitamin loss during storage
items.content: Vitamin C is sensitive to light and heat, so keep the product in a cool place.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy cooked peppers cold in salads, add them to hot soups and stews, use them as sandwich fillings, or serve as a side dish drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked peppers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑size bags – they will retain flavor and nutrients.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato (batata) is a starchy root vegetable rich in carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals. When baked with added fat, it becomes tender, aromatic, and slightly caramelized. It is commonly used as a side dish, in salads, or as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato belongs to the Convolvulaceae family and is not closely related to regular potato.
It contains more beta‑carotene than carrots, giving it a vivid orange color.
Baking with a small amount of fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and E.
Cultures worldwide prepare sweet potato in many ways, from sweet desserts to savory dishes.
Sweet potatoes can be cultivated in warmer climates than regular potatoes.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contains vitamins C and E
items.content: These antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate glycemic impact when baked with fat
items.content: The added fat slows carbohydrate absorption, making it a better option for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat increases the energy density, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Allergy to sweet potato
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience an allergic reaction.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Sweet potatoes contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked sweet potato can be served hot as a side, tossed into salads, used as a filling for tacos, or as a base for vegetarian burgers. Cubed pieces work well in stews and casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑size bags – it retains flavor and texture for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Liquid yogurt is a fermented dairy product made by culturing whole milk with live bacteria Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. It has a smooth, creamy consistency, a mild tangy flavor, and is often fortified with vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Liquid yogurt is commonly consumed as a drink, making it convenient for on‑the‑go consumption.
In some countries (e.g., Russia) the term “kefir” is sometimes used for similar fermented drinks, but true kefir contains different cultures.
The probiotic content can help improve gut microbiota balance.
Flavor and aroma vary with added ingredients such as fruit, honey, vanilla, etc.
Liquid yogurt is used in smoothies, sauces, and marinades.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and teeth health.

items.title: Source of probiotics
items.content: Live cultures may aid digestion and strengthen the immune system.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein helps maintain muscle mass and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt provides riboflavin (B2) and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low‑fat options
items.content: Reduced‑fat liquid yogurt is suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires complete avoidance.

items.title: Added sugar in flavored versions
items.content: Sweetened varieties increase calorie count and can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liquid yogurt can be drunk on its own, blended into smoothies, used as a base for sauces and dressings, or poured over cereals and muesli.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in the original container. After opening, seal tightly and do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
